questions.stem: From which language does the word "semantic" originate, and what does the root word mean?
questions.explanation: Semantic comes from the ancient Greek sēmantikós, meaning significant; semantics is the study of reference, meaning or truth.

questions.stem: For what sole purpose is a semantic layer built in the data world?
questions.explanation: In the data world, the semantic layer is built for the sole purpose of supporting business users, converting complex data models into a simple and user-friendly interface.

questions.stem: Where does a semantic layer sit in relation to the physical data structures?
options: As a representation layer on top of databases, schemas, tables and columns
questions.explanation: A semantic layer is the representation layer on top of databases, schemas, tables and columns, so business users without technical know-how can drag and drop required details on dashboards.

questions.stem: What must be done first before exposing databases, schemas, tables and columns in BI tools for drag and drop?
options: Assign business names to all of them
Move them to a data lake
questions.explanation: For drag and drop, one must first assign business names to all databases, schemas, tables and columns before exposing them in BI tools.

questions.stem: A column named Date could actually contain Date_Of_Birth, Transaction Date or Financial_Year_End_Date. What does this example illustrate?
options: The need for a heat map
Why converting column, table, schema and database names to business understanding is the semantic process
questions.explanation: Converting data models and column, table, schema and database names as per business understanding is the semantic process; a column named Date alone is ambiguous.

questions.stem: How does the semantic layer help when a person's date of birth has different value to life insurance versus medical insurance?
options: It stores two copies of the column
It clarifies the meaning so both parties have a common understanding of its value
It hides the column from one of the parties
It converts the date to a different format for each
questions.explanation: The same column can have different meanings for different parties; the semantic layer bridges this gap by providing a common understanding of the data.

questions.stem: Why did creating semantic layers become difficult after the rise of big data?
options: Because BI tools stopped supporting semantic layers
Because big data includes semi-structured and unstructured data, unlike structured sources where we already knew what was coming
Because business users no longer needed dashboards
Because the Greek root word changed meaning
questions.explanation: In the past semantic layers on structured data were easy because we knew what was coming from source systems; with semi- and unstructured big data, exposing data to business users without a semantic layer became difficult.

questions.stem: What is a Universal Semantic Layer (USL)?
options: A separate semantic layer created for each business unit
A semantic layer that only IT can view
A layer that replaces BI tools entirely
A generic layer supporting all business units and departments so everyone can refer to one USL
A semantic layer limited to structured data
questions.explanation: USL provides a generic layer to support all business units and departments, replacing the earlier practice of separate semantic layers per business unit or department.

questions.stem: What does a Universal Semantic Layer require in order to be built properly?
options: Proper Metadata Management including a Data Dictionary and Data Glossary
A point-to-point integration between all applications
A separate data warehouse per department
questions.explanation: Building a USL is not easy and requires proper Metadata Management, including a Data Dictionary and Data Glossary.

questions.stem: Who creates and maintains the Semantic Layer?
questions.explanation: The Semantic Layer is created and maintained by IT folks.
